title: Receiving thanks gracefully
description: “Oh, it was nothing” sounds modest and lands as a small rejection; there is a kinder way to be thanked.

body.heading: Deflection is a door closing
paragraphs: When someone thanks you and you bat it away — “It was nothing,” “Anyone would have,” “You’d do the same” — you are, however gently, telling them their gratitude is mistaken. They came to give you something and left holding it.
Most deflection is habit, not humility. Underneath it is often discomfort at being seen doing something good, which is worth examining rather than obeying.

body.heading: The gracious receipt
paragraphs: Receiving well is a short skill: pause, let it land, and answer the thanks itself. “You’re welcome — I’m glad it helped” is complete. If it is true, you may add what it gave you: “Honestly, I enjoyed it.” That is not arrogance; it is closing the circuit so the warmth reaches both ends.
If others helped too, pass the thanks along by name. Credit forwarded is credit doubled.

body.heading: Why it matters beyond manners
paragraphs: People repeat what gets received. A workplace, family, or friendship where thanks lands well becomes a place where help is offered more freely — because offering it feels good all the way to the end of the transaction.
Let yourself be thanked. It is the final, easiest part of being helped, and you owe it to the thanker.

takeaway: Let thanks land: pause, accept it plainly, and pass credit along by name.
